notes.claim: A capacitor in series with the start winding makes that winding's current lead the supply voltage, while the main winding's current still lags, so the angle between the currents grows.
The angle is almost 80 degrees against about 30 degrees in a split-phase motor; ideally the capacitor is chosen so the start winding's current leads the main winding's by 90 degrees at startup.
Starting torque goes with the sine of the angle between the currents, so going from 30 to 80 degrees alone raises starting torque to nearly twice that of a split-phase motor.
A capacitor-start motor has moderate starting torque, higher than split-phase, and the phase shift is greater.
The centrifugal switch takes the start winding and capacitor out at about 75 to 80% of speed.
The motor then runs on the main winding alone. His sheet credits 'momentum from the startup'; the fuller source says the auxiliary winding is optional once started.
A permanent-split capacitor motor keeps a continuously energised auxiliary winding and has no centrifugal switch; a larger capacitor can be used just for starting if switched out at speed.
A failed capacitor is one of the most common causes of a motor that hums but will not start; compare a measured capacitor value with its marked rating.

sources.title: Electrical Tech Note — 313
sources.quote: A high value capacitor installed in series with the auxiliary winding shifts the auxiliary winding current ahead of the running winding current to achieve magnetic field rotation during starting.

sources.title: Your motor sheet: the capacitor-start motor
sources.quote: This capacitor causes the current in the auxiliary winding to be out of phase with the current in the main winding, creating the necessary rotating magnetic field.

sources.quote: Ideally, choose a capacitor so that the current through the second winding (IS) leads the current through the main winding (IM) by 90 o at startup (s = 1).

sources.quote: It is then obvious that the increase in the angle (from 30 degrees to 80 degrees) alone increases the starting torque to nearly twice the value developed by a standard split-phase induction motor.

sources.title: Electrical Tech Note — 313
sources.quote: A capacitor-start motor has moderate starting torque, higher than a split-phase motor, and is suited for many applications.

sources.title: Electrical Tech Note — 313
sources.quote: The current phase shift between the auxiliary winding and the main running winding is greater for a capacitor-start motor than for a split-phase motor.

sources.quote: This gives the motor the high starting torque required for heavy loads.

sources.title: Your motor sheet: the capacitor-start motor
sources.quote: Once the motor reaches about 75–80% of its rated speed, a centrifugal switch on the motor shaft automatically disconnects the auxiliary winding and the start capacitor from the circuit.

sources.title: Your motor sheet: the capacitor-start motor
sources.quote: The motor then continues to run on the main winding alone, with the momentum from the startup keeping it going.

sources.title: Electrical Tech Note — 313
sources.quote: There is no centrifugal switch for this type of motor since the auxiliary winding is continuously energized.
